questions.q: Describe an occasion when you got up very early
questions.answer: One morning I got up much earlier than usual to travel with my family to Samarkand. We wanted to arrive with enough time to enjoy the day without rushing from place to place. My alarm went off while it was still dark, and for a moment I wondered why I had agreed to the plan.  I got ready in silence so I would not wake anyone who was still sleeping. We set off before sunrise with a simple breakfast packed for the journey. At first I was sleepy, but watching the sky become brighter through the window gradually lifted my mood. There were fewer vehicles on the road, and we could travel at a steady pace. By the time we arrived, the city was becoming busy and we had almost the whole day ahead of us.  Getting up early was worth it because it gave us more time to explore. We could stop for tea and take our time rather than constantly check a schedule. I did feel tired later in the afternoon, so I would not make a habit of sleeping too little. Had we left several hours later, we might have spent more of the trip worrying about what to miss. The experience showed me that an early start can make a day feel longer when it is planned sensibly. I went to bed early that evening with vivid memories of the journey.  I remember stopping for a quick breakfast after arriving and feeling pleased that we were not already behind schedule. The early start had taken some pressure off. If I repeated the trip, I would still prepare the night before so the morning remained calm. I would also make time to rest later. What makes the memory meaningful is not that everything went exactly to plan. In fact, dealing with a few unexpected moments made the experience more personal, and I think that is why it has stayed with me for so long.

questions.q: Describe an athlete who performed well in an important event
questions.answer: A sportsperson whose performance impressed me is a young player I watched in a local football final. I do not know his name well enough to give a full biography, and the match was not a national event. What stayed with me was how he behaved when his team was under pressure.  In the first half he missed a good chance, and the crowd reacted loudly. For a moment he looked disappointed, but he got back into the game and continued to support his teammates. Later, when the other team pressed forward, he made a careful pass that created an opening. A teammate scored from the move. I was impressed that he did not try to take all the credit afterwards; he pointed to the team and the work they had done in training. The final minutes were tense, but they held on to their lead.  I call his performance successful because it involved more than one good moment. He recovered from a mistake, made a smart decision under pressure and helped others play well. I cannot know how he felt inside, but from the stands he appeared determined rather than panicked. The event reminded me that an important performance is rarely perfect. What counts is whether you can stay involved when something goes wrong and contribute to a shared result. I left the match admiring his attitude as much as his skill.  A younger player nearby watched him after the missed chance and applauded when he made the decisive pass. That response stayed with me. The athlete had set an example by continuing to contribute when it would have been easy to dwell on one error. What I value most is the way this person behaves when things do not go according to plan. Seeing that up close has influenced the standards I set for myself, and it is probably why the relationship has stayed so important to me.

questions.q: Describe a health-related article you read
questions.answer: I read an article about how poor sleep can affect concentration in teenagers. I found it while looking for ways to organise my study routine, since I had noticed that staying up late made difficult reading passages feel even harder the next day. The article was written for a general audience, not as personal medical advice, and I read it with that distinction in mind.  It discussed the link between sleep and attention and suggested keeping a regular schedule. I liked that it explained the reasoning rather than offering a dramatic shortcut. At the same time, I checked the source because online health claims can sound confident even when they are weakly supported. I also noticed that the piece did not pretend every tired student has the same problem. If someone has persistent symptoms, a general article cannot replace professional advice.  What I took from the article was a practical question: was I giving myself enough time to sleep before blaming my concentration on a difficult subject? For a week I tried to put my phone away earlier and notice the difference. That small experiment did not answer every question about health, but it helped me pay attention to my habits. I would recommend reading such articles critically, avoiding sweeping claims and asking for help when needed.  I would be careful not to draw a medical conclusion from my own one-week experiment. The article helped me ask better questions about my routine; it did not diagnose a condition. For any ongoing difficulty, I would seek qualified guidance rather than rely on a single webpage. What makes the memory meaningful is not that everything went exactly to plan. In fact, dealing with a few unexpected moments made the experience more personal, and I think that is why it has stayed with me for so long.

title: Worked with others on a project

questions.q: Describe a time you collaborated on a project
questions.answer: I once worked with two classmates on a short presentation about reducing waste at school. We were given a week and had to explain one practical change rather than list every environmental problem. At first we had different ideas: one person wanted posters, another wanted more bins, and I wanted to focus on how students could find clear information.  We divided the work fairly after agreeing on a shared aim. I drafted the outline, one classmate gathered examples and the other prepared the slides. Halfway through, we realised that our presentation had become too broad. We cut less relevant points and built a clearer argument around labelled collection points and simple instructions. We then rehearsed together so the transitions between speakers would feel natural. When one slide failed to load, we made a backup version rather than hope the problem would disappear.  On the day, each person knew what to say, and the teacher asked a useful question about who would maintain the collection points. We had not fully considered that, so we admitted the limitation and suggested discussing it with school staff. That answer was more honest than pretending our plan was complete. The project taught me to listen to different ideas and solve problems as a team. I enjoyed seeing how separate pieces of work could come together when we kept a common goal in mind.  After the presentation, we kept the slides and notes in a shared folder so each of us could review the feedback. Our idea needed more thought, but the process had strengthened our teamwork. I would happily work with them again on a project with a clearer, manageable scope. Looking back, I remember the small details more clearly than the final result. If something similar happened again, I would probably be less anxious about getting everything perfect and more willing to enjoy the experience as it unfolded.
